transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

I spend so long checking and fixing how I look before work that I’m missing shifts and still feel like my face looks completely wrong. It's gotten to the point where I'm really struggling to even leave the house because of it.
Is your worry and checking behavior focused entirely on how you think your face looks, or do you also have other repetitive routines or unwanted thoughts unrelated to your appearance?

Yes, it is completely focused on my face—specifically how crooked and swollen my nose looks and how uneven my jaw is. I get stuck in these endless loops of checking the mirror, taking selfies, and adjusting my makeup or hair over and over. I don't have any other repetitive routines or unwanted thoughts that aren't about how I look.
When you struggle to leave the house, is it because you worry others will notice and judge your nose and jaw, or do you have a general fear of socializing and embarrassing yourself for other reasons?

I'm not generally afraid of socializing at all. It's just that I'm terrified of people seeing my crooked nose and uneven jaw, and judging how messed up my face looks under those bright lights. I can't stand the thought of everyone staring at those specific flaws.
When people tell you that your nose and jaw look completely normal, do you think there is any possibility they might be right, or are you 100% certain that your face is deformed?

Even when my sister tells me I look fine, it is incredibly hard to believe her. My crooked, swollen nose and uneven face look so glaringly obvious in the mirror and in photos that I'm completely certain these flaws are real. It's really distressing because it feels impossible that they aren't there, and I don't understand why others can't see what is so clearly wrong with me.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a severe preoccupation with imagined or minor physical defects (a crooked, swollen nose and an uneven jaw), accompanied by repetitive behaviors such as excessive mirror checking, taking selfies, and adjusting makeup. These symptoms cause significant functional impairment, leading to missed work shifts and difficulty leaving the home. Although the patient's beliefs are held with delusional intensity (100% certainty), the clinical picture is characteristic of Body Dysmorphic Disorder, which is classified under F45.2 (Hypochondriacal disorder/Dysmorphophobia) in ICD-10. F22 (Delusional disorder) is a key differential diagnosis due to the delusional nature of the somatic beliefs.
